title: Walking through Architectural Spaces: The Impact of Interior Forms on Human Brain Dynamics
research_question: This study investigated the neurophysiological correlates of different interior forms on the perceivers' affective state and the accompanying brain activity during active exploration of virtual architectural spaces.

participants.description: 15 healthy right-handed volunteers (8 females, 7 males), mean age 28.6 years (σ = 2.6), without prior education in architectural studies, normal or corrected to normal vision, no history of neurological disease. Two subjects removed due to technical problems.
participants.recruitment: Volunteers were compensated 10 Euro/h or received course credit for their participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 69 virtual rooms (W x L x H: 5.0 x 7.5 x 3.0 m) with white interior color and identical lighting. These rooms were constructed based on 17 formal clusters of interior forms (plus one simple cubic comparison room) derived from a previous cluster analysis of 343 residential interior images. Each cluster represented different densities of form features (8 types, 13 geometries, 6 scales, 5 locations, 6 angles). Participants walked through these rooms using a head-mounted VR display (HTC Vive).

mechanisms: The Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) is involved in emotional, aesthetic, motor control, cognition, and arousal, showing a fast impact (around 50 ms) of architectural forms on brain activity.
The ACC's role extends to processing architectural features (e.g., surfaces with attachment type, 2D rectangular geometries) beyond their emotional impact.

The Posterior Cingulate Cortex (PCC) and occipital lobe are involved in processing different room perspectives and changes in room depths, reflecting spatial orientation and visual processing during movement.
Natural movement and active exploration of architectural spaces contribute to embodied perception and influence brain dynamics.
moderators: Arousal ratings (controlled for in partial correlations)
Pleasure ratings (controlled for in partial correlations)
implementation_implications: Natural movement is the best way to investigate brain dynamics underlying natural perception and affective processes associated with perceiving a 3D environment.
The MoBI approach combined with VR can systematically develop architectural studies to understand the impact of design on human experience.
limitations: The study design faced a trade-off between the time participants spent in a room to explore interior aspects and develop an affective response, and the number of room trials that could be collected for EEG analyses, potentially leading to non-optimal signal-to-noise ratios.
Future studies should increase the number of room trials by focusing on selected clusters to improve signal-to-noise ratio.
